analysis.one_liner: Helps coal miners with black lung disease win benefits faster, raises their payments, and holds mine operators financially responsible.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had six Democratic Senate sponsors, never received a committee hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul the federal program that pays benefits to coal miners disabled by black lung disease. It would give miners free government-funded medical evaluations, create an automatic approval for miners with the most severe form of the disease, raise and inflation-adjust their monthly checks, help pay lawyers' fees for slow-moving claims, and let miners reopen cases denied based on X-rays later discredited. It would also tighten rules for coal companies that self-insure their benefit obligations, raising penalties from $1,000 to $25,000 and holding executives personally liable when a company defaults.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal miners with black lung disease and their surviving spouses and dependents. Miners with severe disease (progressive massive fibrosis) would be approved automatically without proving total disability. All claimants would get government-paid medical evaluations, help with legal fees on claims stuck for more than two years, and monthly benefits that rise with inflation instead of being frozen when federal pay is frozen. Miners whose earlier claims were denied using X-ray readings later discredited could file new claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal miners with black lung and their survivors

how_it_helps.text: Creates an irrebuttable presumption of total disability for miners diagnosed with the most severe form of black lung (progressive massive fibrosis), confirmed by X-ray, CT scan, biopsy, or autopsy [S2].

Requires the Labor Department to provide claimants a free complete pulmonary evaluation, including CT scans where warranted, paid for from the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, with the responsible coal operator reimbursing the fund if benefits are awarded [S2].

Raises the annual benefit to $9,627.60 starting in 2024 and indexes it to inflation, replacing a formula tied to federal employee pay that produced no cost-of-living increases in years with federal pay freezes [S2].

Establishes a program paying attorneys' fees (up to $4,500) and unreimbursed medical expenses (up to $3,000) for contested claims not resolved within two years, with the liable operator reimbursing the fund; the Government Accountability Office found only 42 percent of claimants have an attorney at the initial stage [S2].
Lets miners and survivors reopen denied claims where a negative X-ray reading came from a physician whose interpretations the Secretary has directed not be credited [S2].

Requires new self-insurance standards for coal operators, including financial-health criteria and annual security requirements, and raises the penalty for failing to secure benefit payments from $1,000 to $25,000, extending personal liability to executives and companies under common control when an operator defaults or goes bankrupt [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Coal mine operators, which would face higher penalties, stricter self-insurance requirements, and potential personal liability for executives when companies default on benefit obligations; and the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which advances the cost of medical evaluations and fee payments and is reimbursed by liable operators. The trust fund is financed by a tax on coal production.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal mine operators and the federal trust fund

drawbacks.text: The indexed benefit increase and the government-paid evaluations and fee program add obligations to the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund in the short term; the fund is financed by a coal production tax, and recovery from operators depends on their solvency — the bill's own findings note companies have defaulted on self-insured obligations [S2].

The stricter self-insurance rules, higher penalties, and expanded personal liability for executives raise compliance and financial costs for coal operators, costs that in a struggling industry could weigh on margins and employment [S2].

The automatic benefit presumption for severe disease and restrictions on which physicians may perform claim evaluations shift decision-making toward the government and away from company-retained examiners, which operators would characterize as tilting the claims process [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits are real but modest in dollar terms: the new base benefit of roughly $9,600 a year replaces a similar amount and mainly protects it from inflation. The larger practical gains are procedural — free medical evidence development, help with lawyers, and reopening of claims tainted by discredited X-ray readings — in a claims system the bill's findings describe as complex, adversarial, and stacked against miners. The main cost is greater financial exposure for coal operators and short-term demands on the trust fund, which the bill addresses by seeking reimbursement from liable operators.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health and labor committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Casey introduced the bill on November 15, 2023, with five Democratic cosponsors: Fetterman, Kaine, Warner, Manchin, and Brown [S2].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; no further action appears in the record [S1] [S4].
The bill received no hearing, no markup, no floor vote in the Senate, and no House action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal operators that self-insure their black lung obligations without adequate collateral keep the status quo, and miners with black lung continue facing the adversarial claims process the bill's findings described, with trust fund taxpayers continuing to backstop defaulted company obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal operators; miners' claims stay as they were

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote in either chamber [S2] [S3].

industries.note: Operators would face stricter self-insurance standards, penalties raised from $1,000 to $25,000, and personal liability for executives and commonly controlled companies when they default on black lung obligations. The bill's findings state that many operators self-insured without proper collateral and defaulted, pushing costs onto the public trust fund.

industries.industry: Physicians performing claims examinations for coal companies
industries.note: The bill bars from the government's qualified-physician list any doctor employed by or recently retained by a party opposing a claim, and allows readjudication of claims based on X-ray readings the Secretary has discredited. This would cut off a source of paid expert work and unwind prior favorable evidence.

industries.industry: Black Lung Disability Trust Fund (taxpayer-backed backstop)
industries.note: The fund would advance new costs for evaluations and fee payments, but gain from operator reimbursements, higher default penalties, and stricter self-insurance rules designed to keep companies from shifting liabilities onto it.
